description: Express the positivity domain uniformly for both signs of $b$: if $b>0$, keep $�delta>-1/b$; if $b<0$, keep $\delta<1/|b|$; for $b=0$, $n(\mathbf{x})=\bar n$ and the sampled bias is zero. Introduce $\alpha=1/(|b|\sigma)>0$ for $b\neq0$ so all retained-domain Gaussian integrals can be written with the same upper-tail or lower-tail probability $�Phi(\alpha)$ after the change of variable $z=\operatorname{sgn}(b)\delta/\sigma$.
reasoning: The positivity constraint is $1+b\delta>0$. For $b>0$, this gives $\delta>-1/b$; with $z=\delta/\sigma$, the lower limit is $z>-1/(b\sigma)=-\alpha$. For $b<0$, the constraint is $\delta<1/|b|$; with $z=-\delta/\sigma$, this again becomes $z>-1/(|b|\sigma)=-\alpha$. Because $z$ is always standard normal under this change of variables, the retained-domain probability is the same Gaussian tail $\Phi(\alpha)$ in both cases. The special case $b=0$ is trivial: the field is constant and the bias vanishes.
result:
For $b\neq 0$, define $\alpha\equiv 1/(|b|\sigma)>0$ and let $z\equiv \operatorname{sgn}(b)\,\delta/\sigma$. Then the clipping condition $1+b\delta>0$ becomes a single retained-domain inequality for both signs of $b$:
$$
z>-\alpha.
$$
Equivalently, the surviving Gaussian mass is always the same tail probability
$$
P(1+b\delta>0)=\int_{-\alpha}^{\infty}\frac{dz}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-z^2/2}=\Phi(\alpha).
$$
If $b=0$, there is no clipping, $n(\mathbf{x})=\bar n$, and the sampled bias is zero.
